c.tagline: Taiwan's laid-back middle city and the birthplace of bubble tea.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are plentiful, metered and cheap; Uber and LINE Taxi both operate and let you pay by card, but street taxis usually want cash.

emergency.note: 119 reaches fire and ambulance; 110 is the police. English may be limited, so ask a local to help if possible.

hood_landmark.West District (Xiqu): National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts, Taichung

hood_desc: Taichung's cultured core, with the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts, the green Calligraphy Greenway, indie bookshops, boutiques and hand-drip cafés; the best walkable base for first-timers.
The historic old downtown around the ornate 1917 Baroque train station, Miyahara ice cream, temples and budget guesthouses; atmospheric and being revived, though quiet at night.
Home to the giant Fengjia Night Market plus modern malls and the Feng Chia University crowd; the city's liveliest area for street food, shopping and going out.
A leafy district around Taichung Park, the Confucius Temple and universities, with the Yizhong Street student shopping strip; central, green and lively with a young feel.
A large, mostly residential district on the city's northeast with markets, parks and the Dakeng hiking trails nearby; quieter and more local, good value for longer stays.
lodging: Golden Tulip Zhong Xin Hotel Taichung

water.note: Tap water is treated but locals boil or filter it; drink boiled or bottled.

transit.hours: The MRT Green Line runs roughly 6:00 AM to midnight; city buses run into the late evening, with taxis and Uber covering the small hours.
transit.note: The single Green Line links the HSR station in Wuri to Beitun via the city; buses (free for the first 10 km with an iPASS) still cover most of the sprawling city, and YouBike shared bikes fill short gaps.
transit.pay: Get an iPASS or EasyCard (about NT$100) from any convenience store or metro station and tap on the MRT and buses; city bus rides are free for the first 10 km with the card. Single MRT tokens are also sold at station machines.

bus: Intercity coaches (Kuo-Kuang, UBus) to Taipei and Kaohsiung
train: Taiwan High Speed Rail (Taichung/Wuri HSR station)

transit.m: City bus toward Taichung centre / HSR station (~40-60 min)
Taxi to the city centre (25-35 min)

tip.r: Tipping is not customary in Taiwan; some hotels and higher-end restaurants add a 10% service charge, so nothing extra is expected.

food.name: Sun cake
food.desc: Taichung's emblem pastry: paper-thin flaky layers around a soft, buttery malt-sugar centre, best eaten warm from the bakery.

places.name: Taiyangtang
places.note: One of the founding sun cake bakeries on Taichung's pastry street.

places.name: Chen Yun Peng Sun Cake
places.note: Rival veteran baker a few doors down; try both and pick a side.

places.name: Miyahara
places.note: Sells sun cakes and pineapple cakes in elaborate gift boxes.

food.name: Braised pork rice at the Second Market
food.desc: Fatty soy-braised pork over rice, eaten at communal tables inside a 1917 market hall that is a Taichung institution.

places.name: Shanhe Lu Rou Fan
places.note: The market's most queued-for stall; sells out well before closing.

places.name: Taichung Second Market
places.note: Historic hexagonal market packed with old-guard breakfast counters.

food.name: Radish cake
food.desc: Cai tou guo: griddled blocks of steamed radish cake with egg and a sweet-savoury sauce, a Taichung breakfast ritual.

places.name: Wang Ji Cai Tou Guo
places.note: Decades-old stall famous for crisp-edged radish cake with egg.

places.name: Taichung Second Market
places.note: Neighbouring stalls sell it alongside rice noodle soup and rou geng.

food.name: Crispy fried chicken cutlet
food.desc: A flattened chicken breast fried to a shattering crust and dusted with pepper and chilli, sold in a paper bag the size of a face.

places.name: Fengjia Night Market
places.note: Taiwan's biggest night market and the testing ground for new snacks.

places.name: Yizhong Street Night Market
places.note: Student market with a denser, cheaper run of fried snack stalls.

food.name: Fengjia street snacks
food.desc: Fengjia is where many Taiwanese snacks were invented: sausage-in-sausage, Fengjia pancakes, stinky tofu and oyster omelette.

places.name: Fengjia Night Market
places.note: Stalls open from late afternoon and run past midnight; busiest 7 to 10pm.

places.name: Zhonghua Road Night Market
places.note: Older, smaller street market strong on grilled squid and pao pao ice.

food.name: Miyahara ice cream
food.desc: Dozens of ice cream flavours built on Taiwanese fruit and tea, scooped inside a restored Japanese-era eye clinic.

places.name: Miyahara
places.note: Choose scoops plus toppings; the interior alone is worth the visit.

places.name: Dawn Cake
places.note: Related Taichung pastry brand known for its pineapple cakes.

food.name: Bubble milk tea
food.desc: Tapioca pearls in iced milk tea were invented in Taichung in the 1980s, and the city still treats the shake as a serious craft.

places.name: Chun Shui Tang Siwei Original Store
places.note: The shop credited with inventing bubble tea; sit-down tea house menu.

places.name: Fengjia Night Market tea stands
places.note: Dozens of competing stalls testing new toppings and tea bases.

food.name: Sun Moon Lake black tea
food.desc: Assam-descended black tea grown a couple of hours from the city, drunk plain or as the base of Taichung's milk teas.

places.name: Miyahara tea counter
places.note: Sells loose-leaf Taiwanese teas in tins plus tea drinks to go.

places.name: Chun Shui Tang
places.note: Serves the tea straight as well as shaken, a good side-by-side tasting.

landmarks: Rainbow Village
A tiny veterans' settlement saved from demolition by nonagenarian 'Rainbow Grandpa' Huang Yung-fu, whose riotous painted murals cover every wall and pavement.
National Taichung Theater
Toyo Ito's architectural marvel of curving cave-like walls without a single straight column, one of the world's most innovative opera houses.
Fengjia Night Market
Taiwan's largest night market, a neon maze near Feng Chia University where thousands of stalls launch the island's newest street-food crazes.
Miyahara
A 1927 Japanese-era eye hospital reborn as a Harry Potter-esque emporium of bookshelf-lined halls, famous pineapple cakes and extravagant ice-cream sundaes.
Luce Memorial Chapel (Tunghai University)
I.M. Pei and Chen Chi-kwan's sublime 1963 chapel, four sweeping conoid walls of golden tiles rising from the university's shaded campus lawns.
Taichung Park
The city's graceful 1903 park, whose twin-pavilioned Huxin Pavilion floating on the lake remains Taichung's official emblem.
National Museum of Natural Science and Botanical Garden
Taiwan's premier science museum, paired with a rainforest glasshouse conservatory, anchoring the leafy Calligraphy Greenway cultural corridor.
Chun Shui Tang Teahouse (original branch)
The birthplace of bubble tea, where pearl milk tea was invented in the 1980s, still serving pilgrims of Taiwan's most famous drink.
921 Earthquake Museum of Taiwan
A sobering, brilliantly designed museum built over a school destroyed by the 1999 quake, preserving buckled tracks and collapsed classrooms in situ.
Calligraphy Greenway
A 3.6-kilometre tree-lined pedestrian corridor linking the Natural Science Museum and Fine Arts Museum, dotted with public art and pocket gardens.

train.note: THSR bullet trains from Taichung/Wuri station reach Taipei in about 1 hour and Kaohsiung (Zuoying) in about 50 minutes; conventional TRA trains run up and down the west coast from Taichung Station.

bus.note: Frequent intercity coaches (Kuo-Kuang, UBus, Ho-Hsin) link Taichung with Taipei (~2.5 hrs), Kaohsiung and other west-coast cities from the Chaoma and city bus terminals.

ferry.note: Taichung Port at Wuqi, about 25 km west of the centre, is principally a container and bulk terminal; its passenger building was built for the cross-strait fast ferry to Pingtan in Fujian, but that service has not run to a regular schedule since the 2020 border closures. No scheduled domestic ferry sails from Taichung either. For the Penghu islands, use Budai in Chiayi (about 90 minutes' crossing, summer season only) or the year-round Taihua ferry from Kaohsiung operated by Taiwan Navigation; both ports are 1-2 hours from Taichung by train.
